speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Within days of the conflict, Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: It has also attacked close to 20 vessels.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: President Trump has said recently that the US has almost accomplished its goals in Iran, but it is still not clear when the conflict will end and when the Strait will be reopened.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: In the near term, the closure of the Strait has caused a global shortage of energy supplies, including crude oil and gas.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Before the conflict, one quarter of the world's supply of seaborne oil and one-fifth of its gas transited through the Strait.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: More than 80% of these flows were bound for Asia.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Such a severe choking off of supply is unprecedented.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: It is the worst disruption since the 1973 oil embargo.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: The fuel shortages have caused a surge in global energy prices.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: The disruption extends to other key products too, particularly those that use oil and natural gas as feedstock or starting materials.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Most fertilisers are made using natural gas – and the Middle East is a key global producer of fertilisers, second only to Russia.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Nearly a third of the world's fertiliser trade is shipped through the Strait.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: The supply disruption has led to soaring fertiliser costs.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: If farmers reduce or stop fertiliser use, crop yields will fall, raising global food prices.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: This includes aluminium, which is used to manufacture cars, airplanes and many other products, as well as helium, which is needed for producing semiconductor chips and cooling magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) machines.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: These disruptions are cascading through the global economy.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Higher fuel and raw material costs will raise business costs, some of which will pass through to consumers through higher prices.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Higher energy prices have also increased transport and shipping costs.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Airfreight rates between Asia and Europe have almost doubled since the conflict began.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: This will eventually push up costs of other items including food and grocery supplies.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Rising business costs and consumer prices will, in turn, dampen demand and slow down the global economy.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Many Asian currencies have weakened against a stronger US dollar, compounding inflation and growth risks in these countries.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: All of these pressures could intensify further in the coming weeks.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: As a small and highly open economy, Singapore will not be able to insulate ourselves completely from this crisis.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We must respond with a coordinated, multi-agency effort to cushion the impact on our people and our economy.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: This is why we have convened the Homefront Crisis Ministerial Committee (HCMC), chaired by Coordinating Minister for National Security K Shanmugam and comprising several Ministers.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: First, securing our supplies, such as LNG and diesel for power, as well as other essential fuel products like jet fuel and motor gasoline; strengthening our economic resilience, by helping businesses to preserve their productive capacity and capability, and facilitating their transformation where necessary; providing targeted help for those most affected by the crisis, including businesses in the energy and chemicals cluster, platform workers and low-income families; and helping workers with training and employment support, as well as providing households with broad-based help to address cost-of-living concerns.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Minister Shanmugam will share more later on how we are organising ourselves to coordinate our national response.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Early data indicates that economic activity continued to be resilient in the first quarter of 2026.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: However, growth in the coming quarters is likely to be affected by the ongoing conflict.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: While the conflict impacts many sectors, some sectors will feel it more than others.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: In manufacturing, the most direct impact will be on industries that rely on natural gas, crude oil and crude oil derivatives as feedstock.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Our refineries have adjusted by reducing their run rates and brought in shipments from sources outside of the Middle East.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Some firms, such as PCS have already declared force majeure due to upstream supply disruptions.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Beyond the energy and chemicals cluster, higher fuel and electricity prices will also affect a wider range of industries, including electronics, precision engineering and other energy-intensive clusters.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: In services, outward-oriented sectors like air and sea transport, as well as tourism, will be affected by higher costs and weaker demand.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: On the other hand, domestically-oriented sectors, such as retail, food services and private land transport will face higher operating costs, including utilities and fuel.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Taken together, these sectoral impacts will weigh on economic activities in the coming quarters, although the extent remains uncertain as the conflict is still unfolding.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: MTI will continue to monitor developments closely and will update our GDP forecast in May.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: As we import nearly all our energy, the spike in global oil and natural gas prices will inevitably raise fuel and electricity costs for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: About 95% of Singapore's electricity is generated from natural gas, whose price is mostly pegged to market prices.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: The increase is modest relative to the spike in fuel prices.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: But that is because the tariff is based on fuel prices from the first 10 weeks of the preceding quarter, from January to the middle of March.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: That means only a small portion of the recent surge in fuel prices has been captured in this tariff adjustment.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: These cost increases will feed through to broader inflation in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We had earlier forecast Consumer Price Index (CPI)-All Items and Monetary Authority of Singapore's (MAS') Core Inflation to come in at 1.0% to 2.0% in 2026, after inflation broadly eased in 2025.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: However, the Middle East situation has driven up global energy and commodity prices, which will drive up global inflation.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: If the conflict is protracted, higher inflation in our source markets could also lead to further increases in import prices over time.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: These pressures will be felt by households in more expensive electricity, transport and daily necessities.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Lower-income households will be more affected, as a larger share of their spending goes towards essentials.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Even more worrying is the risk of escalation, including further damage to energy infrastructure, or a prolonged blockade of the Strait of Hormuz.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: This could trigger a global energy crunch – slowing global growth and pushing up inflation worldwide.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: This crisis has reminded us again of how interconnected and how fragile the global system is.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We need to be prepared for more frequent inflation shocks and supply chain disruptions in a world of heightened geopolitical contestation.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We will strengthen our resilience by building up inventories and diversifying our sources of supply, but Singapore will always remain dependent on imports for our supplies.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: It is therefore critical that we continue to strengthen our partnerships with like-minded countries and uphold an open and rules-based trading system.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: As a trading nation, keeping faith with our partners and maintaining our credibility is crucial.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We must foster the free flow of energy and goods as far as possible.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Prime Minister Lawrence Wong has spoken to Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: They jointly affirmed our commitment to support the flow of essential goods, including petroleum oils, such as diesel, and LNG between our two countries.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Prime Minister Wong has also spoken to New Zealand Prime Minister Christopher Luxon to reaffirm our commitment to strengthen supply resilience and mitigate disruptions.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Singapore and New Zealand concluded an Agreement on Trade in Essential Supplies last October, which is a timely framework to ensure the continued flow of critical goods between our two countries.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: The Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Foreign Ministers and Economic Ministers have discussed and underscored the importance of maintaining stable, open and reliable global energy supply chains, as well as the importance of minimising disruptions to the flow of essential supplies, including food.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Singapore and 10 fellow members of the Future of Investment and Trade Partnership also issued a Joint Statement last week, reaffirming the importance of not imposing restrictive trade measures, including ex port restrictions, tariffs and non-tariff barriers, on essential goods.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Speaker, this crisis will not end in the short term, and Singapore must prepare early and not be complacent.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: As a small open economy, we cannot be completely unaffected.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Rising external costs will ultimately impact businesses, households and prices.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We will strive to ensure stable energy and food supplies, strengthen economic resilience to cope with the crisis and provide necessary assistance to the most severely affected businesses, platform workers and low-income families.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We will also provide training and employment support for workers and help families cope with cost-of-living concerns.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Most importantly, whether businesses or individuals, all must respond calmly to changes.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: The Government will strengthen inter-agency coordination to safeguard supplies, stabilise the economy and mitigate the impact.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: As we have done before, let us stay resilient and united, as we weather this crisis together.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: (In English): Sir, the Government recognises that the impact of this crisis will be felt by households and businesses.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We will do what is necessary to support them through this period.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Senior Minister of State for Finance Jeffrey Siow will share more on our support measures.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: At the same time, all of us – Government, businesses and households – will need to do our part.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: This also means making our energy and supply chains more resilient, deepening partnerships with like-minded countries and staying open and connected to the global economy.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Acting Minister for Transport and Senior Minister for Finance.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport and Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: I will now explain what the Government is doing to support our businesses, our workers and our households through this period.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport and Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: We could not know about the conflict that would break out in Iran, but we could see many uncertainties ahead and therefore, the need to provide greater reassurance and support in this Budget.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport and Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: Hence, Prime Minister Lawrence Wong announced substantial broad-based support measures, including a Corporate Income Tax rebate, Community Development Council (CDC) vouchers and the Cost-of-Living Special Payment.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport and Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: We provided more support for lower-wage workers and households, such as enhancements to the Progressive Wage Credit Scheme, and better support for lower-income families through ComLink+.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport and Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: We also enhanced U-Save rebates, giving 1.5 times the regular amount – or up to $570 this financial year.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport and Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: The first tranche of U-Save rebates will be disbursed in April.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport and Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: This will help defray the increase in utility bills from April to June.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport and Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: A second tranche of U-Save rebates will be disbursed in July.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport and Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: This should help to defray the much sharper increase in utility bills from July to September that we expect with the spike in oil prices.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport and Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: Sixteen days after the Budget, the US and Israel launched coordinated airstrikes on Iran.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport and Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: This current situation in the Middle East remains highly uncertain.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport and Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: We cannot predict how exactly events will unfold or when the conflict will end.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport and Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: What we do know is that Singaporeans are already feeling some of the effects on the ground.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport and Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: In Singapore, petrol and diesel prices have already risen sharply in tandem with global oil prices and are likely to remain elevated for some time.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport and Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: And while the impact has not yet fully filtered through for items, such as electricity and food, we have to brace ourselves because we know, from experience, that this will come.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport and Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: We will supplement what was announced at the Budget with a further package of support measures.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport and Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: These provide targeted support to those who are the most heavily and directly affected.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport and Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: We will also provide broad-based support for businesses and households.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport and Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: The sharp increase in fuel prices had an immediate effect on the earnings of platform workers, private hire car drivers and taxi drivers.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport and Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: The National Trades Union Congress (NTUC) has worked with platform and taxi operators on fuel vouchers and fare adjustments, which have helped to cushion the impact.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport and Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: For certain essential bus services, such as those for school students, seniors and persons with disabilities, the Government will provide temporary assistance to co-fund cost increases, to enable these services to continue operating without disruption.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport and Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: The respective Government agencies will provide more details.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport and Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: Several Members have asked if the Government will consider reducing fuel or diesel subsidies across the board.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport and Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: We do not think this is the right move.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport and Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: It is too blunt an approach and it could also be regressive.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport and Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: At the same time, we want to preserve the price signals for consumers to use energy more efficiently.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport and Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: More fundamentally, as an open economy, we must allow fuel prices to reflect market realities.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport and Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: If prices are artificially suppressed, importers may choose to divert fuel to where prices are higher and over time, this can tighten supply and leave us worse off.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport and Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: Instead, our targeted approach provides direct support to those who are directly affected and this allows us to channel more help to those who need it most.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport and Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: Second, let me talk about support for businesses.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport and Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: Higher energy and logistics costs will continue to be felt by businesses across the economy for some time.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport and Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: Our small and medium enterprises (SMEs), in particular, are more vulnerable to sudden cost increases.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport and Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: We will also raise the minimum benefit that a company with at least one local employee will receive, from $1,500 to $2,000.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport and Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: The total benefits cap for each company will be raised from $30,000 to $40,000.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport and Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: We will disburse this enhancement quickly, as early as the end of this month.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport and Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: Even as we roll out immediate relief, this challenging period is also a timely reminder for all our businesses to build longer-term resilience against high and sustained energy prices.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport and Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: Businesses that invest in energy efficiency will reduce their exposure to volatile energy prices and lower their long-run operating costs.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport and Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: We currently have an Energy Efficiency Grant which applies to six designated sectors, for example, food services, retail, manufacturing and construction.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport and Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: Additionally, some companies in the Energy and Chemicals sector have been badly affected by feedstock supply disruptions.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport and Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: Our agencies are engaging these firms and assessing how best to provide targeted support to preserve critical capabilities for our economy.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport and Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: This includes major Government infrastructure projects, such as the Cross Island Mass Rapid Transit (MRT) Line and new Housing and Development Board (HDB) Build-To-Order (BTO) projects.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport and Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: The Building and Construction Authority (BCA) will issue a circular with more details shortly.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport and Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: Third, let me talk about support for households.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport and Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: We are tracking the prices of food and other essential goods and services very closely.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport and Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: So far, rising fuel prices have not yet fully percolated into wider price increases across the economy.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport and Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: But given the uncertainty in the Middle East, it is still too early to update our projections of inflation in Singapore, or to quantify the full impact on households.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport and Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: This will bring the total quantum of the Special Payment to between $400 and $600 per person.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport and Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: (In Mandarin):   With tensions in the Middle East and rising energy prices, we understand Singaporeans' concerns.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport and Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: The Government announced several support measures today to provide timely help for our people.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport and Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: We will also strengthen assistance for those most directly affected.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport and Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: For example, taxi drivers and platform workers will receive a cash relief of $200 from the end of April.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport and Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: The Government will also provide more help for businesses and households, including by bringing forward the disbursement of the $500 CDC Vouchers from January 2027 to June this year.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport and Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: The Cost-of-Living Special Payment assistance to be distributed in September will also be increased by $200.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport and Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: We still do not know how long this crisis will last nor do we know how big the impact will be.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport and Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: But the Government will continue to closely monitor the situation and take additional measures when necessary to help Singaporeans.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport and Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: The Government has always managed national resources prudently and responsibly, building up Reserves first.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport and Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: Therefore, when crises arise, the Government has the capability to help our people, ensuring no one is left behind.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport and Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: Regardless of what kind of crisis we encounter, as long as everyone unites and works together, we will be able to overcome the difficulties.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport and Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: (In English): Mr Speaker, the Government has put together a substantial first response to the energy crisis caused by the Middle East conflict.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport and Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: We do not know how long the conflict and its economic impact will last.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport and Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: But the Government is alive to the situation.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport and Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: It is much larger than our immediate response in 2022, after war broke out in Ukraine and caused a similar surge in oil and gas prices.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport and Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: To fund these measures, the Government will work within the amount approved in the Supply Act last month in the first instance, and seek Parliament's approval for the supplementary budget later on.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport and Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: What Singaporeans can count on is a Government that is well-prepared, builds sufficient buffers, anticipates problems and thus is ready and able to respond swiftly with solutions.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport and Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: We will always make sure that no Singaporean is left to bear his or her burden alone.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Coordinating Minister for National Security and Minister for Home Affairs.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for National Security and Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The HCEG reports to and receives directions from the HCMC.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for National Security and Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Its role was set out and explained in Parliament in 2004 by then-Minister for Home Affairs Mr Wong Kan Seng.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for National Security and Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Structurally, and organisationally, from the time it was set up, the Minister for Home Affairs has been designated as the chair of the HCMC.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for National Security and Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Deputy Prime Minister Gan is the Advisor to this HCMC.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for National Security and Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The key Ministries and their Ministers all play an important role.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for National Security and Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We have also brought in newer officeholders to complement the team.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for National Security and Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They will bring additional perspectives as they deal with specific issues related to the ongoing situation.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for National Security and Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Members may also access these materials through the MP@SGPARL App.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There are 13 members in this HCMC and their names are in the Annex.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Over the past month, both the HCMC and the HCEG have met several times.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The HCMC has been looking at a broad range of issues, including energy and food resilience, including supply chain resilience; resilience for other essentials; security developments, both domestic and external; support measures for Singaporeans and public communications; and foreign affairs and our diplomatic relations.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In response to the heightened threat environment, from the security perspective, we have put in place additional measures.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Immigration and Checkpoints Authority (ICA) has increased checks at our checkpoints upon the escalation of the conflict, and Police have also stepped up patrols at areas of concern.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We also activated contingency plans to repatriate Singaporeans in the Middle East affected by the conflict.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Flights were organised by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MFA) and the Ministry of Defence (MINDEF).

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They were executed at short notice and required close coordination between the Ministries.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: MFA began assessing evacuation routes upon the escalation of hostilities, given the possibility of prolonged airport or airspace closures in the region.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Ministry of Culture, Community and Youth (MCCY) and the Islamic Religious Council of Singapore (Majlis Ugama Islam Singapura or MUIS) have also been engaging Singaporean residents in the Middle East, as well as key partners, such as the Association of Muslim Travel Agents Singapore, for Umrah and Haj arrangements in the light of this conflict.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You have heard about the impact of the conflict from Deputy Prime Minister.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Many other critical supplies pass through the Strait of Hormuz, including helium and aluminium.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We can no longer rely on such supplies in the same way.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I will speak in a little more detail about two key sectors: first, fuel and energy; and second, food supplies.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Since the start of the conflict, several countries have announced export restrictions on fuel or implemented fuel rationing measures.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So far, there has been no need to do so.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Global energy majors and trading companies have a sizeable presence in Singapore.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We are the world's third largest oil trading hub and the sixth largest refinery export hub.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is the result of a deliberate long-term strategy.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Today, they underpin our energy and fuel resilience.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Because of this, we are deeply connected to global flows of energy.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That gives us access to diverse sources of energy and fuel supplies.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, we are able to respond to disruptions more flexibly.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We continue, so far, to have access to crude oil.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And we have been meeting our domestic needs and international obligations for fuels.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: However, we do not know how long the disruptions will last.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As Minister Tan See Leng said a fortnight ago, we need to brace ourselves for a bumpy ride ahead.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: No one can say what the situation will look like, or will be like if there are more serious disruptions and if they last longer.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We have secured crude oil supplies from alternative sources.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But we have to pay prevailing prices, which are much higher.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Singaporeans are feeling the impact in higher prices as fuel and energy costs rise.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Prices are likely to remain high even after hostilities cease.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Damage to infrastructure in the Middle East will take time to repair.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We have already seen damage to large oil facilities in Saudi Arabia, Bahrain and other places.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Even if the Strait of Hormuz fully reopens tomorrow, global oil and gas export capacity will not return to pre-conflict levels quickly.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In the broader term, we are concerned about broader disruptions to global supply chains which can affect goods critical to Singapore's economy and essential services.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: MTI is monitoring the situation closely and working with the industries.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As for electricity, we have taken steps to reduce risks to disruption of our supplies, to meet our electricity needs.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Apart from the Middle East, we also import LNG from Australia, one of our key suppliers; the US; and Mozambique.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: GasCo was set up last year to centralise gas procurement for the power sector.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Second, while 95% of our electricity is generated from natural gas, our power plants can switch from natural gas to diesel when needed.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: These reserves comprise a mixture of natural gas and diesel.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We are also planning to increase our fuel reserves.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It will be costly, but we think it necessary.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We have so far not tapped on our fuel reserves nor have we implemented fuel rationing.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Energy Market Authority (EMA) also requires power generation companies to have pre-arranged contractual access to additional fuel.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Fuel suppliers are required to deliver the fuel to the power generation companies within a set number of days upon activation.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And we are prepared, if necessary, to direct the power generation companies to exercise their legal rights to secure the additional fuel.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That said, securing the additional fuel by the power generation companies may be subject to force majeure events.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Some of the additional fuel may be sourced from overseas and may be subject to supply disruptions again.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This ensures that they are sufficiently hedged and will be better able to handle an extended period of gas price volatility.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The position we put ourselves in before the crisis and the steps we have taken since the crisis have helped us remain relatively stable.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: However, this remains a low-probability scenario for now, though we continue to monitor developments closely.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Deputy Prime Minister spoke earlier on the regulated electricity tariff.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Even though the cost of gas accounts for almost half of the regulated tariff, this has so far only partially transmitted to the tariff price.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If the conflict is prolonged, then we have to expect much sharper increases in electricity prices.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The situation has caused many countries to take a closer look at their energy security.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I will make two points on our situation.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As I said earlier, we are a major refining centre.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: When countries began imposing controls on their export of fuel, many asked us if we would still be able to supply them with refined fuel products.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Some of these countries supply crude oil and other essential products to us.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In turn, we supply them with refined products, which they need.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It keeps Singapore relevant in the international energy trade.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And this has enabled us to have continued access to crude oil.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Some have also questioned the role of refineries over the medium term, given our green transition.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But as stated before, our path to net zero will depend on technological breakthroughs and sustained international cooperation.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: For now, the priority worldwide is energy security.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Countries everywhere need to keep the lights on.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Fossil fuels remain part of the global energy mix.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Because renewable energy is not yet able to meet all of the demand.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In that context, Singapore will continue to play a role as a refining hub.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And we will continue to work with our refineries to improve their energy efficiency and reduce their carbon footprint.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Second, we must continue to press on with our efforts to diversify our sources of energy.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: At the Committee of Supply debate in March, the Government announced that it would raise the target to three gigawatt-peak.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In the near term, we will continue to deploy solar energy domestically and pursue electricity imports from the region.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In the medium to long term, we are assessing other sources of energy to diversify our fuel mix.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Advanced nuclear energy technologies have the potential to provide safe, reliable and clean baseload power.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Nuclear fuel is energy dense and can be efficiently stockpiled.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But adopting nuclear energy requires very serious consideration.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It needs to be studied very carefully to ensure that it is safe for deployment in or around Singapore.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We have been building up the technical expertise to evaluate the technology as it develops.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And we are partnering overseas governments and companies who are leaders in this field.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We really need the best expertise on this.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We will continue to study this very carefully and rigorously.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And there are dedicated teams in the Government that are doing this.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Our primary concern is with inflationary pressures on our food products.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Natural gas is a key feedstock for fertilisers.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: With disruptions to gas supply, fertiliser prices will go up.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Food crops and animal feed will therefore cost more, and the price of our imported food products will rise.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As fuel costs go up, it will also cost more to transport and store food products.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That will help us mitigate the impact of any unforeseen supply disruptions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Meanwhile, we are relooking at our supply chains with a view towards strengthening them.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: However, we are only able to maintain stockpiles of essential food types.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Singaporeans should be prepared for supplies of some foods from some countries to be unavailable and will have to exercise flexibility in choosing alternatives.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There have been questions about the extent of Singapore's fuel reserves and food stockpiles.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As a policy, we do not disclose these.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Disclosing such details would reveal where our limits lie and that could be used against Singapore in times of crisis.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: What matters is that we have sufficient buffers and contingency plans in place.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And we regularly review and strengthen these arrangements to ensure that they remain robust.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We will respond as a whole-of-Government to take care of Singapore and Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We will work together to get through the crisis and emerge stronger – as we always have.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: I earlier said that several Members have asked if the Government will consider reducing fuel or diesel subsidies.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: It is the exact opposite of what I actually said, so I thought I should clarify.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Before I call on hon Members for clarifications, I just wish to point out that pursuant to Standing Order No 23, Members may seek clarification on the Ministerial Statements, but no debate shall be allowed thereon.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Members can seek your clarifications by way of asking questions.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: So, I seek Members' understanding to keep your clarifications clear and concise so that the Ministers can answer as many clarifications as possible.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Likewise, I will ask the Ministers to also keep your answers clear and concise.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: To make our discussions clearer, more focus and efficient, I propose to structure our clarifications as follows.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: These could include petrol, electricity and their impact on trade and the economy.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: The second group of clarifications will include the impact on local businesses and households and the support measures for them.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: And the third group of clarifications will be on general security issues and related matters.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: So, I ask for Members' cooperation to group your clarifications according to the subject matters I have listed.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: This will give clarity to our discussions, make it easier to follow and understand the answers provided, and allow for deeper and more focused examination of the issues and suggestions from Members.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I assure Members that I will give you sufficient opportunity to make your clarifications on the different topics.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: There is no need to make all your clarifications at once.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Once again, the first basket of clarifications will be energy and trade-related matters.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I will then move on to the second group of clarifications on the impact on local businesses and households and the support measures for them.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: And finally the third group of clarifications will be more security issues and related matters.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I have three clarifications related to the first set of questions, Mr Speaker.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: My first supplementary question: Singapore is a price-taker.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: With the Middle East situation, there are unknowns.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The concern is whether seafood is regarded also as an essential in the Government's definition.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Third, I noticed that our measures, as the Senior Minister of State has shared earlier, are calibrated in some ways.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is also a testament to our long-term focus in terms of macro policy mix.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I think the Senior Minister of State mentioned there is always a possibility and ability to do that, but what is the possibility of off-Budget measures coming?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But I think it is very important for us to continue to maintain our strong Singapore dollar policy to control inflation pass-through.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As I have stated earlier, inflation pass-through is of utmost importance.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Speaker, given the brevity of time, I will dispense with the thanking.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: I will take the first question on energy and his point about the fact that we are price-takers and how we are thinking of the possibility of the risks of export restrictions by some of our partners.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Perhaps to curate the point more, I think you are referring specifically to natural gas, because that is how we are powering up our entire country and our economy.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We import natural gas primarily through piped natural gas from our immediate neighbours like Malaysia, as well as LNG from around the world.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: At this particular point in time, there is no upstream disruption from the piped natural gas supply.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: For LNG, we continue to source the whole world through GasCo, which, if Members recall, it was the previous Government, in this Chamber, that we pass an amendment to our Electricity Act, allowing us to form GasCo and then to centralise the procurement of gas.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We source them from Australia, from the US, from Mozambique and even as we speak, we continue to look for new markets.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: For us, diversification has always been one of the key strategies.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Of course, we also now look for alternative sources, renewable energy or otherwise, but that will take a bit more time.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Having said that, we have also ensured that our generation system, our generation companies (gencos) can run both on natural gas and on diesel.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: So, in the event that we do not have enough natural gas, the gencos will be required to switch to diesel to run and power up.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We have also established stockpiles, but as I have also shared before, given the constraint of land that we have within our country, there is a fiscal limit as to how much stockpiling we can do.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Of course, we have also explored whether we could put it on the waters, get these very large crude carriers or use the floating storage regasification units.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: But then again, space and the cost to maintain these very large crude carriers would not be, at this particular point in time, that economically feasible.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: But I want to assure the Member and all Members of the House that we constantly establish close relationships, dialogues, conversations with like-minded partners.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The key in point, as the Deputy Prime Minister shared, our Prime Minister has also issued a joint statement with the Prime Minister of Australia, Prime Minister Albanese, to establish ties and to ensure that we can continue to get supply of LNG from Australia.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: On seafood specifically, we do not see immediate risk.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: We have also got local production of seafood readily available.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: At this point, as both the Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister have shared, our main risk for agriculture lies in fertiliser.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: And in the short term, no impact, but we think there could be secondary impact, as the Member has shared with diesel and other energy prices, just with other sectors.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: So, we are monitoring the situation and we will keep everyone posted as things happen.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Supaat, your question on the support measures, I will defer it to the next bucket for Acting Minister Siow to respond.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In a Facebook post about a week ago, the Minister-in-charge of Energy, Science and Technology warned about the possibility of fuel shortages that could not be ruled out in the medium to long term, and that Singaporeans and businesses should prepare for significant turbulence in the months to come; and the Minister also projected up to a five-year repair time for Qatar's LNG facilities.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The second question pertains to energy security more generally.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Does the war in the Middle East present an opportunity to potentially bring forward Singapore's plans of acquiring more renewable energy sources, such as hydroelectricity from our neighbours and in larger quantities than had been previously planned?

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I mentioned the fuel shortages potentially ahead, because the threat of the escalation of the crisis in the Middle East is very real.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: If we follow the tweets, if we follow all of the news that is coming out, whether it is from the US or from Iran, from Israel, we can pretty much come to that same conclusion.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, it is important for us as a country that while we can take some calm, but we should also be very pragmatic and very real about what the challenges are.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: And the fact is that because we do not produce any of these natural resources on our shores, we therefore have to be prepared for a possible worse-case scenario, not worst case, but a worse-case scenario compared to what it is today.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: And to that end, we constantly reach out to our immediate neighbours to talk about piped natural gas (PNG), the continuous supply of PNG.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: But at the same time we also establish a more diversified source country strategy so that it strengthens our position in terms of our resilience.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Some of the existing fields that we are drawing from, inherently, are also faced with dwindling reserves, within those reservoirs that we are tapping from.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Of course, we are also discussing with our neighbours about the potential of exploring new areas for us to tap into.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, I hope to give some positive news, but we are stepping up.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Today, I am not at liberty to share that first.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Where we are, I cannot predict how long more this war will take.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: And what I think we should be sure about is that because we are open, we are connected.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: While this is an advantage for us, given the 150 oil majors that we have here, the third largest oil trading hub in the world, the sixth largest refinery complex in the world, but upstream, the crude still has to come from somewhere.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: And if the Middle East as a source is choked, we will still not necessarily have that significant impact, but the impact downstream is that it will take a longer time for crude from other parts of the world to bypass the Middle East to come to us.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The quality of the crude, they are also different.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: And because of the differences in the quality of the crude, the run rates of our refinery complexes would also therefore have to be optimised.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, it is this whole cascade of the different refinery processes that we also have to take into account that is contributing, in some cases, amplifying this crisis.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: But our modus operandi has always been, we do not impose export restrictions and we will still abide by the rules-based global trading framework.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Given that the current energy crunch is disproportionately impacting Asia, does the Minister see this as opportunity to strengthen regional cooperation in energy resilience, including exploring ASEAN collaboration in nuclear energy, such as joint investments and joint operations in the nuclear power plant?

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We certainly see an opportunity in every crisis.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: It is precisely what all of us do.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Our entire team, fellow political officeholders, Government Parliamentary Committee members, that we constantly outreach to our like-minded partners to work even more closely with them.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The most recent visit two weeks ago to Japan with the Prime Minister, last week's visit to Australia and there will be many more of such outreach to many of our like-minded partners.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: On the nuclear energy collaboration, it is not for want of or lack of trying.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I think the Member will appreciate the fact that because we are so small and as the Coordinating Minister for National Security alluded to just now, we have to ensure that these advanced nuclear energy technologies are safe.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: It is just that there has not been a single site of deployment yet.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I mean, there are some that is in the process of being commissioned, for instance, in China, and there are some coming up in the US.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We can be a fast adopter, but we cannot be the first-of-a-kind mover.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I hope that gives the Member the context of what we are doing.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: So, can I ask the Minister if he can share about why this phenomenon of diesel is being more expensive than petrol?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The Minister earlier shared that the Government's gencos can actually switch from gas to diesel.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: So, is that the reason why diesel has gone up because of the Government procurement of diesel?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: So, how can we enable or incentivise our other businesses to do that to help companies that are impacted by the cost increases of diesel?

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I mean the ongoing tensions involving Iran, as I have said a few times already, significantly increase the uncertainty and, of course, the risk to oil supply.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: And it pushes up the crude oil all over the world.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: If you compare diesel, diesel is a very versatile fuel mix, because the strong demand from transport, from the shipping industry, and there is also some limited refining capacity that is possible using diesel.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: And as I have shared with you, even our combined cycle gas turbines, which the gencos use, can use diesel as a back-up.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: You will appreciate the fact that it is also easier to store diesel compared to natural gas, because the boiling point of natural gas, I think it is probably about minus 150 over degrees Celsius.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, to keep natural gas, you need that energy to keep it at that level.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: And if you put it in a floating storage regasification unit, there is a lot of boil-off of that gas.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: LNG is not an easy fuel for you to store unlike diesel.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: When you talk about stockpiling, of course, a significant proportion of that amount is in diesel.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, you can appreciate that because of the versatility and in farm tractors in many of the agrarian countries around, that emphasis has always been on diesel.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: That is why it has risen faster compared to petrol.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: As far as the roll-out of support measures, Acting Minister for Transport Jeffrey Siow has already shared what are the measures.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: MTI will continue to keep a close watch on this space and if need be, the Government will not hesitate to come in, to act, to help.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: And thirdly, what is the status of Singapore's helium supplies following the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, and whether the Government has contingency plans to help the semiconductor industry access sufficient helium supplies for production and also, does the Government foresee any delays in MRI procedures or increases in the price of MRIs for the rest of the year as a result of shortages in helium?

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Helium is used in small quantities as a cooling agent in MRI machines.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: They do not get topped up very frequently.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: I will take the question on helium for semiconductor.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: For the semiconductor sector, helium is used mainly in wafer fabrication for heat management, cooling and process stability.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: By and large, the wafer fabs here have a multi-source strategy for helium supplies.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: And wafer fabs in Singapore, in particular, they have, so far, not expressed immediate operational impact, but have started to activate more alternative supplies.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: We will continue to work closely with the industry to monitor their needs.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: The question on security, the part about Strait of Hormuz and Iranian authorities, Minister Vivian Balakrishnan, do you want to answer now or do you want to do it at the last part?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I suggest we do at the last part.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Fadli Fawzi, I will direct the question to Minister Vivian Balakrishnan later.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I declare that I work in the logistics arm of the port.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: First, will the measures to support the domestic transport and critical sector extend to the logistics and supply chain sector, such as the hauliers, as well as the port, because this is certainly a critical sector during this period?

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Second supplementary question: the war accelerates a fundamental global supply chain shift that has been happening for several years, away from cheapest, fastest and the leanest to safest, most resilient, as well as the most trusted.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: So, the Economic Strategy Review recommendations are timely and should be implemented swiftly.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But my question is, are they bold enough and do they go far enough in view of what has just happened in the Middle East?

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Will Singapore be able to not just survive disruption, but thrive because of it as a reliability hub for our region?

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: Speaker, I would like to respond to Mr Fadli Fawzi's earlier question on petrol prices at the petrol stations.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: Singapore has a competitive and open economy, and prices naturally would fluctuate in response to various factors, including changes in global supply and global demand.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: Instead, the Government's approach is to ensure that the market remains competitive.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: For the petrol stations, we also know that there are several players in the market.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: At present, there is no evidence to suggest that the market structure is not competitive.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: The entry of Cnergy operated by Union Gas is also an encouraging sign, as it provides more choices to consumers.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: The first is on the port and port services, and whether they can be considered as critical services.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: As I mentioned in my speech, what the Government agencies will do is to assess whether or not such services are critical parts of what we have to do and whether the direct impact of these services is due to the rise in prices.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: So, in this case, the Maritime Port Authority of Singapore (MPA) will assess that and make a case to the Ministry of Finance (MOF) for support.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: On the Economic Strategy Review, indeed, I agree with the Member that there are opportunities for us to look at.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: One of the key things that we are looking at through the Economic Strategy Review is how to strengthen Singapore as a hub of flows.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: I think the energy crisis reiterates for us how important that strategy is.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: It is precisely because that Singapore is in the middle of energy flows that we are able to have energy security and to be able to be in the position that we are in.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: I just wanted to clarify, in modelling some of these scenarios regarding our fuel sufficiency, I was wondering if these assessments include more materially longer or more severe kinds of scenarios than we typically model.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: And whether or not, the price reflects supply and demand, whether there is a price threshold and the duration for which the price of the commodities are sustained for that we are monitoring, before we implement more rationing measures.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We simulate models across chronological parameters as well as geographical parameters.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, our simulations run, particularly for power generation, our scenarios run on if one region is completely choked versus two regions versus multiple regions.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I am not at liberty to share because it is a function of our own national security.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The parameters go into a lot of details, in terms of which are the sectors that are most exposed and then which are the sectors that get indirectly influenced by the cascading effect, and then to the more domestic sectors getting influenced.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: One of the key things is that our civil servants are very, very well adapt in managing all of these different scenarios.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Like I said, I cannot go into the details because it is a matter of our own security.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Supplementary question one: what is the Government's assessment of the overall food supply situation and how the does Government stabilise the prices of essential food items and curb profiteering, so that seniors and also low-income families can still afford their meals and food expenses?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Supplementary question two: the local bus transport companies are badly affected by the surge in diesel prices, and they are running diesel cost increases of more than $1 million per month for some of them.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: However, they are also bound by the prices locked in their contracts and are not able to increase their prices.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: These local transport companies are essential to ensure our workers can get to work on time.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Other than transportation for school children and people with disabilities, how would the measures help such local transport companies tide through this crisis, especially if the war prolongs?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Supplementary question three: jet fuel supply has been severely affected and fuel prices have surged dramatically.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: The sustainable aviation fuel levy has been postponed to apply for flights from first January 2027 onwards.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: How will the impact on fuel supply and fuel prices impact Singapore as an air hub, especially if the war prolongs?

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: Speaker, I would like to respond to Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh's question regarding price threshold.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: This may not be a fair way of distributing our limited resources.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: It will also reduce the incentive for Singaporeans, as well as businesses to switch to more energy efficient modes of transport.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: Instead, the Government's approach is to ensure that our fuel market remains well-functioning and competitive, so that fuel companies are incentivised to compete, innovate and become more efficient.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: On electricity prices, on whether it is a price threshold, the electricity prices is something that the Government will continue to watch closely because it affects households and businesses directly.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: Again, our priority is to make sure that there are enough support measures, such as U-Save, CDC vouchers and targeted support measures for businesses that are more affected by the electricity price increase.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: We are working with the aviation stakeholders to monitor the fuel supply for aviation hubs carefully to ensure that it remains stable.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: There are no significant supply shortages for now as we have adequate fuel supply from the diversified sources.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: But if higher fuel prices persist, this will lead to increased cost pressures, which may filter to passengers and consumers in various sectors.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: We note that some airlines have made commercial decisions to raise ticket prices in response to the soaring cost of fuel.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: These remain commercial decisions which we do not intervene in.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: However, we will continue to work closely with the industry to monitor the situation and assess whether there is a need for the Government to take further measures.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Due to our efforts in partnership with other governments, for example, Thailand and Vietnam for rice cooperation, New Zealand and Australia for other food areas, as well as working with the industry to diversify our food sources over the years, importers can now pivot more readily to alternative sources, if needed.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: If the situation worsens and food imports are severely disrupted, the stockpile of essential food items, as shared by the Coordinating Minister, that we have been maintaining and expanding will provide us time to restore food flows and sustain our population.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: This multi-pillar approach ensures that Singapore is able to meet our food needs and Singaporeans can continue to experience reasonable normalcy during disruptions.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: However, we also have to recognise that in a crisis, we will have to prioritise our efforts.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: It will not always be possible to have everyone's favourite food or favourite brand in every disruption, but what we can do is to provide the assurance of food supply where it matters most.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: The Government is monitoring the developments in the Middle East and its impact on Singapore's food supply closely.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Singapore imports most of our food and from many different sources – we have 180 countries and regions that we import from.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: And food coming from major ports, such as the Strait of Hormuz, accounts for even less, at less than 0.5%.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: However, as global food supply chains are interconnected, we cannot rule out eventual disruptions to our food supply if the conflict persists.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: In his Ministerial Statement, the Deputy Prime Minister mentioned that the closure of the Strait of Hormuz would have an impact on other key products, including fertilisers.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: This, in turn, could translate to lower agricultural yield down the line and potential supply disruptions.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: So, we are monitoring this and the food supply situation very closely.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: We will keep up our diversification, global partnerships, local production and stockpiling efforts as required.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Since the start of the Middle East conflict, the Singapore Food Agency has also stepped up our engagements with importers and retailers to share information on possible risks to food supply, so that they may activate alternative sources early and when needed.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: We stand ready to activate our existing arrangements with partner countries to ensure that food continues to flow as needed too.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: We want to support our local farmers, especially now, to weather this crisis, and we will help them to increase their market share for certain food types, which will strengthen Singapore's food resilience in the long term.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: And as they say, never waste a good crisis.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Senior Minister of State Zaqy, have you finished?

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: For now, the Government will help citizens through support measures, such as CDC vouchers and also the Cost-of-Living Special Payment.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: However, we need to be prepared for what happens next.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: It may begin as an energy crisis, but it could develop into larger supply disruptions across many sectors, including the food sector.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Our cooperation with other governments as well as industries has given us the opportunity to further diversify our food sources, and this means that food importers can pivot to other sources easily.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: If the situation worsens, we have food supplies – our stockpile – to sustain our population.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Local farms can also increase their production further and provide fresh food supply to us.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: So, we still have food supply to meet our needs.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: As the Government increases our diversification efforts, global partnerships, local production and stockpiling efforts as needed, we will get ready to try to diversify our sources and make adjustments to our habits and lifestyle.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: We have received feedback from transport associations on the impact on local bus services and we are working very closely with them to smoothen out the impact on these bus services.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: As I mentioned, where the bus services are critical, we will co-share the cost of these services, but for others that are more general, we will work with them to smoothen out the impact.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: We will expect some pass-through of the cost to the consumers, just like my colleague Senior Minister of State Murali mentioned, through airfares.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: And broadly, we will support the bus companies through the business measures, for instance, like the Corporate Income Tax rebates that I had talked about in my speech.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: And on the consumer side, we are also supporting through the payments like the Cost-of-Living Special Payment, which can be used to defray some of these costs.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: There are still many Members who have raised their hands.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Can I again request Members for this first bucket, keep it to the energy, trade and industry matters?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: We will move on to support measures after this.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: While we are not an IEA member state, this is a widely recognised global benchmark for an emergency on energy resilience.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Could the Minister confirm if Singapore's oil stock levels meet this international standard to provide greater assurance for Singaporeans and businesses?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: And I will note that I am not asking for us to reveal all our cards, but just our adherence to this international standard.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: (In English): "Energy is not easy to obtain.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Given the war in the Middle East, there is also the possibility of simultaneous disruptions both at the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab-el-Mandeb Strait of the Red Sea.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Could the Government elaborate whether such a double chokehold situation is explicitly considered and what are the consequences?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How do these scenarios translate into pre-emptive measures that safeguard both supply continuity and household affordability?

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We think that a simultaneous choke or blockade of the Red Sea near the Gulf of Aden, where the Houthis from South Yemen – which is also something that I did highlight in my Facebook posts about a week ago – would not have a significant impact, because it primarily impacts supplies coming from Europe through the Suez Canal.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I note that amongst the different sources of energy, diesel prices have risen much higher than electricity prices.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: And diesel fuels many commercial operators, including buses and lorries, which feeds into many other sectors.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, does the Minister think that this is a good time for operators of commercial businesses to switch from diesel trucks and lorries to friendlier, electric vehicle (EV) versions?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: And if so, would any incentives be given for such switches to make it easier to change capital, which is, of course, a long-term investment?

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: A function of why the electricity tariffs seem to have risen slower compared to diesel is, as I have shared, in fact, Deputy Prime Minister shared early on, how the regulated tariff is calculated – based on last quarter's prices of natural gas, which is benchmark to the Brent crude benchmark index.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: From January to February, the war broke out on 28 February, so we have only factored in, at most, about half a month of that price increase.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: While I thank the Member for that supplementary question, because I am going to leverage on this supplementary question to let everyone know, and I have put up a harbinger – it is not insider trading, because I think it is an open secret that the prices have gone up significantly – for household consumers, for domestic consumers, if they want to hedge, they may want to switch to a fixed price contract moving forward.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: For businesses, how they are going to convert the diesel trucks, the diesel vehicles to EVs, I think for them to perhaps move out of their trucks today to convert it physically, I think it would take a lot of time.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I am not an engineer, so I would not know what is involved in that.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Of course, if they want to trade it off and buy an EV instead, I think that is an option that is available.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: As far as any subsidies and so on are concerned, I think this is not something that I can comment on.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Suffice to say that for some of the businesses, if they want to convert to more energy efficient measures and so on, there is the Energy Efficiency Grant.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: For the larger ones, there is also the Resource Efficiency Grant for Emissions as well.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I would think that these businesses can find out more about which are the ones that they are eligible for and make the applications accordingly.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I think Acting Minister Siow would like to respond as well.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: There are companies that have already made use of the grant.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: But we have this grant and we will encourage companies to make use of it, to switch to more energy efficient vehicles.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Building on the point that the Minister-in-charge of energy had raised earlier about fixed rates.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: There is concern amongst consumers that the gencos and the electricity suppliers may, at some point, invoke a force majeure, and that would affect the supply contracts that are signed with consumers.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Therefore, I seek clarification, what safeguards there are in place to protect consumers and businesses from disruptions and the dramatic price spikes, and how will the Government ensure continuity of supply and fair contractual outcomes for consumers as well as the gencos?

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Indeed, I think that is a valid concern.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: EMA has been constantly engaging all the gencos.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
