text: Today, supply at this point in time, is not an issue because we have got GasCo, which has sourced for supplies and diversified the various sources of supplies quite broadly.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: If anything at all, I think the force majeure portion comes because the pricing of these LNG cargoes coming in, has gone up significantly, compared to pre-crisis times.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, many of the contracts that they were locked in, they can no longer supply, because obviously, the feedstock has gone up significantly.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: And this is where EMA has stepped in to form the bridge between these large consumers, together with the gencos.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Our sense today is that the domestic consumers, because they form not a very big part of the gencos' exposure, if I am not mistaken, I have to check this, but I think they use less than four megawatts for the entire year.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, I do not think they will be affected that much.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: That is, the next few quarters will see significant increase in the tariffs.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This is something that is food for thought for everyone.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Not long after the electricity market liberalisation in the early 2000s, the Government actually favoured vesting contracts as a regulatory safeguard for price spikes over price caps or a capacity market.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I believe such contracts were eventually expected to be phased out, once sufficient competition was assured.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And I understand that this tool is meant to regulate competitive marketing and not crisis-related shocks.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Nevertheless, given the current development, I wonder if the Minister would be willing to share: if the mechanism is still in play today; whether it covers a full extent of electricity demand in Singapore; if this mechanism is indeed active for the current Strait of Hormuz crisis, and if so, what the current gap between the vesting and wholesale market prices is; and finally, how much he believes the safeguard has passed through to the open retail market, given that price increases observed in February were about 10%?

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: As I have shared earlier on, for those gencos which have entered into very long vesting contracts, I think some of their clients and customers would already find it hard to keep and maintain those kind of pricings.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Hence, these are the ones that we are currently managing to try and understand the impact.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: It is actually this group, potentially, that may invoke the force majeure clause.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Having said that, today, a lot of the cargoes that we are buying in are on spot price.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: To your question as to how this would impact, we do not have all the necessary details at this point in time.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Perhaps, at the next Parliamentary Sitting, I would invite you to file a Parliamentary Question.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We can get into a more robust presentation at that point in time.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: One, does the Government detect any early signals of job losses arising from the new disruption?

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: Two, does the Government detect any early signals in terms of wealth inflows into Singapore, given our status as a wealth hub?

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: And three, does the Government detect any early signals with regard to Singapore's status as an aviation hub?

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: If the answer is yes, what is the Government's position and what is the Government's response?

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: In case you are wondering, I am still the Minister for Manpower, notwithstanding, the entire discussion was just on energy.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: What we have done is to work very closely with MTI and the Economic Development Board for the affected power generation refinery and the energy-intensive emission sector to ensure that there is no permanent scarring.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We will continue to help workers in those particular sectors.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We have not completely ironed out the plans.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Again, if the Member is interested, he can file a Parliamentary Question and we can elaborate on that more.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: For the rest of the signals, perhaps I can invite my other colleagues to take on the questions.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Apart from the disruptions, most of Changi Airport's flights have been operating normally.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: The disruptions have been limited to some Singapore-Middle East passenger and cargo services.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Airlines have also added flights between Singapore and other regions, such as Europe, to cater to demand in the wake of the reduction in flights to the Middle East.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: The situation now still remains fluid and uncertain.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: It is too early to determine if longer-term network reconfigurations will take place.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: We will continue to work closely with the industry to monitor the situation.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Singapore has been a financial centre and we have been a centre to receive capital and wealth investment from all over the world.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: There has been increased interest and enquiries with regard to wealth coming into Singapore.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We are happy to see that trend and we are also happy that we are able to provide services to these investors and this capital, that we can allow them to have an alternative location to be able to continue to safekeep their wealth and also, use Singapore as a gateway to invest in this region.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: I think we will continue to monitor the situation, and we will continue to ensure that we operate efficiently and reliably as a financial centre.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Quite a lot of the questions that are being asked are rather similar and I can see the answers are also getting rather similar.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Can I request that unless you have something really specific which have not been addressed before, please raise your hand?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: My supplementary questions draw from the fact that the situation displays: one, how Singapore has agency; and two, how Singapore can use the situation as a catalyst.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: On agency, how can Singapore use its sterling status as an oil trading hub and a critical oil refinery centre to create agency, to trade with Australia, for example, for enhanced LNG, or New Zealand for food supplies?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Here, I declare that I am a lawyer in private practice who represents oil companies and oil refineries in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: On the second point, as for us being able to use the situation as a catalyst, how can the crisis offer itself as a catalyst for Singapore to seriously explore nuclear civil energy, provided it is safe?

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I have answered in quite different parts, but perhaps to just curate it for the Member's utility.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: First, indeed, this crisis is also an opportunity for us to build even closer ties, with our reputation, our credibility, our consistency, our predictability and our transparency.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Our relationship with Australia will hopefully be up a few notches when we reassure them that we will abide by a rules-based multilateral trading system, we will not impose export restrictions, and depending on the upstream feedstock that we are able to get and our refineries continue to refine, notwithstanding the fact that there are different types of crude nowadays, but we still try to optimise the refineries' complex operational capabilities to make sure that the downstream supply of essential fuel products – the diesel, the motor gas, together with the naphtha – they continue to get the supply.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Likewise, they are a major supplier, they are the third largest supplier of LNG, that they would also not in any way curtail their exports to us.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I think Minister Vivian may know that better.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: At the same time, we are trying to see how we can accelerate the same discussions with Australia and other countries.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: On nuclear, I have also shared that it is not a question of us not wanting to do it, we want to make sure that it is safe.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The small modular reactors for advanced nuclear energies have proven to be very safe.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We just want to ensure that there is a site that has been planted, is operational and that we can use that as a reference site or model.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: On food price monitoring, given that we import more than 90% of our food supply, could the Government share more – whether there are ways for data on the monitoring dashboard that is used by the Ministry of Sustainability and the Environment to be shared more proactively so that households and businesses have more timely visibility of emerging price trends for scenario planning and whether more forward-looking indicators can be included to help Singaporeans better cope with potential price fluctuations.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As a second point, I thank Minister Tan for some of his sharing in response to questions earlier on contingency scenario planning as well as the stockpile for LNG and diesel.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I understand the need to not disclose sensitive details around our national food stockpile.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, could the Government consider whether there is merit to provide some general indicators of adequacy for certain food items and essentials, such as broad coverage, ranges or scenario readiness, so as to give Singaporeans greater assurance in light of the current uncertainties, similar to the two to three months' data which was shared during COVID-19.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Where I am coming from is while many appreciate these broader updates, there is room to build understanding and make the impact clearer at an individual and household level so that our people have a better understanding how prepared we are but not immune and also a sense of agency that they can still do something amidst this uncertainty.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: The Department of Statistics publishes monthly indices on the import prices of food products.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: This allows us to assess imported food cost pressures that may in turn feed through some of our domestic food inflation and food and beverage services inflation.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: On whether we can have forward-looking indices, I think we will have to continue to monitor the situation and as best as we can, provide timely information to businesses as well as to local households.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Minister of State Zaqy, do you want to respond?

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: (In Mandarin):   Singapore is highly dependent on energy import.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Can Minister tell us whether we will set up and expand our strategic fuel stockpile, and whether our current fuel stockpile is adequate if supply disruption is prolonged?

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The Member is asking whether we can increase our stockpile, whether we have plans to increase the reserves.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I want to reassure everyone that if I had the benefit of space, I would stockpile significantly higher amounts.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Our very real constraint is the space we have here.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: If we stockpile in a foreign country, then I do not think that that is really stockpiling for our own needs if the situation gets very, very severe.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I hope that we can understand that these are real constraints that we have here in our country, and hence, my original exhortation is energy is existential for us; energy is precious; let us try to conserve it.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I am not at liberty to share that because this is our national security, and I beg for your understanding and your indulgence.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Essentially, my question relates to what is the impact of the Middle East conflict on Singapore's air and sea freight, and our transport hubs; we being key maritime and air hubs.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I am grateful that Minister of State Murali has given some answers on the air hub.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I wish to declare my interest as a consultant in a shipping law firm.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I have one supplementary question relating to the air hub and this refers to the deferral of the sustainable aviation fuel levy.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: And as soon as we are able to make further announcements, we will do so.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: My supplementary question is how quick is this switching?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Can it manage the volatility, especially this unprecedented volatility?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: And do we need to re-optimise our power plants to manage our energy generation resilience?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: My second supplementary question is on our refining capability and the feedstock flexibility.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: How adaptable are our refineries to alternative crude grades?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: In a prolonged disruption scenario, do we foresee any erosion of Singapore's competitiveness relative to other refining hubs?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: And similar to what Member Christopher de Souza mentioned, is this an opportunity to strengthen our refining competitiveness beyond the relationships with other countries, but also in our capability to take other feedstock to diversify the source?

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Our gencos comprise a combination of different combined cycle gas turbines.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Some are existing combined cycle gas turbines that would require time for that conversion.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Others, for instance, are using the new J-class and H-class type of combined cycle gas turbines, which can also be at least 30% hydrogen ready.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, because of that spectrum of the number of gencos and the combined cycle gas turbines that we have here, it is not a one size fits all.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: If you recall, the Member was part of the same group of Parliamentarians who passed the Bill.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: What we have done is to effectively strengthen our entire framework since five years ago, where EMA would require the different gencos to show and to indicate to us ahead of time their gas, their supplies, their access to gas supplies, their vesting contracts, and so on.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We, holding the stockpile, would then work with them to work out the time that would be required for that switch from gas to diesel, so as to ensure that there is no outage or unnecessary downtime when they switch over.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, that part of it is something that we work very closely with them on.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: On your second point, what was the second point?

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This is something that I have also learnt over the last fortnight.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I think those of you who are in the oil and gas industry may know it better than I do.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: But we now primarily have access to two types of crude: the sweet crude and the sour crude.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Sour crude means that there is a lot more sulphur and it comes mainly from the Middle East.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: It is more favoured because the downstream products you get, whether it is diesel, naphtha to bitumen, seems to be more versatile compared to the other types of crude.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, what we have done is that there will be some compromise in the refinery capabilities.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: Is this an opportunity to strengthen our refining competitiveness beyond the relationships with other countries?

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Yes, with our team and myself, we have been working to see how we can strengthen this.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I think it also calls for a fundamental pivot in terms of the thinking because we do also at the same time want to decarbonise and work towards a zero-emission target by 2050.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So long as you have the energy-intensive sector, we need to think about how, while we build up, at the same time, we need to have a clear pathway towards decarbonisation.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Having said that, actually our refineries are probably one of the most efficient in terms of carbon emissions.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: But as you step up the refinery, you have to keep up with that level of carbon emissions.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: It is a balance and a trade-off that we will have to consider over the medium to longer term.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I am going to move on to the next group of clarifications.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: This should cover the impact on local businesses and households, and also the support measures for them.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: The measures announced for platform drivers and riders will go some way in easing the pressures on their livelihoods.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: I believe they are currently not covered in the announcement.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: NTUC will stand ready to partner the Government as a stakeholder to ensure that these workers are not left behind.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Second, may I ask if the Government will encourage service buyers to take a fair and practical approach in reviewing existing contracts where sustained fuel cost increases materially affects the viability of our workers' livelihoods.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: I think we will be happy to work with NTUC again to see how that can be done.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: As for service buyers, and whether or not we can help them with the contracts, the Government has already stated its position as a responsible buyer for its own contracts.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: We hope that we can also encourage private sector service buyers, as well as service providers, to also come to reasonable accommodations for these purposes.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: I have two more clarifications on this point as to who may be excluded, and what may be excluded.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: On my first point, for SMEs, some of these energy efficiency machines or equipment may be considered large-ticket items for them.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: So, has the Government considered schemes that can help to co-pay upon purchase orders, or even to pay direct to vendors upon installation of such equipment?

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: My second point is, as Acting Minister Jeffrey Siow mentioned, it is for base-tier equipment.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: My point is, for some SMEs buying, they may have different sources from the pre-approved vendors and equipment.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Can the submissions of new models or new equipment be concurrently considered with the application of the Energy Efficiency Grant, especially in this time when we want to scale up adoption of energy efficiency equipment?

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: Second, we want to get the support out there as soon as possible.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: So, without having to change the scheme parameters significantly, I think what we want to do is just extend the current parameters.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: But we will certainly consider at a later stage whether there are other things that we can do to enhance this in terms of financing.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: And we are happy to take in inputs together with the applications.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: I think today's application process is fairly automatic, but I will check with the economic agency to see whether there is room for us to give room for people to give suggestions on what type of equipment.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: In light of wanting more Singaporeans to also be a part of the movement to manage energy consumption and usage, what are some national initiatives that can be brought back, for example, guidelines on lighting usage in public places or even in commercial buildings in terms of managing energy uses?

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: Second is, what is some of the Government's plan to partner with community organisations to help some residents or Singaporeans who fall through the crack and need a little bit more assistance due to the impact of the crisis in the Middle East?

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: (In Malay):   Earlier, I asked about the support that can specifically be given to communities that are more affected by the outcomes or impact of the Middle East conflict, and we have already heard details about emotional, spiritual and mental support.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: Are there specific platforms or additional support that can be expected, perhaps from self-help bodies as well as MUIS or mosques?

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs and Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: (In Malay):   Mr Speaker, as shared earlier, the Government is dealing with this Middle East conflict through a whole-of-Government effort.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs and Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: We realise that this conflict has raised deep concerns among our community.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs and Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Many may feel alarmed, not just at the human suffering but also about the impact on their families and daily lives, including rising costs.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs and Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: As a small and open economy, Singapore cannot escape the impact of this crisis.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs and Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: The effects of these increases are already being felt in daily life.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs and Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: This conflict will also be felt by Singaporeans, with higher energy and food prices, leading to increased cost of living.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs and Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: We must be prepared for the possibility that these pressures will continue in the months ahead.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs and Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: We will closely monitor the prices of food and goods as well as other essential services.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs and Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: The Government is prepared to provide further support if necessary.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs and Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: For our Muslim community, MUIS is in contact with Singaporean students in the Middle East and providing necessary support.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs and Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: MUIS is also working with partners, such as the Association of Muslim Travel Agents Singapore (AMTAS), regarding umrah and hajj arrangements.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs and Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: We will continue to monitor the situation closely and take necessary measures.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs and Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Most importantly, the safety and well-being of Singaporeans remain our priority.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs and Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: As Deputy Prime Minister Gan said earlier, all of us can play our part.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs and Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: We should do what we can to conserve energy, avoid wastage and be more prudent when using resources.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs and Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: If every household practises these measures, it will make a difference, especially during these uncertain times.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs and Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Let us strengthen our solidarity and remain resilient through these challenging times.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs and Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: We must ensure that global tensions do not create divisions in our society.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs and Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: This is an opportunity for us to draw closer to one another and exemplify the shared values that guide us as a society, to be the best versions of ourselves and for the common good of all Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: This extended to taxis, taxi drivers, private hire car drivers and motorcyclists.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The support rendered included road tax rebates and petrol duty rebates.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Given the elevated prices of fuel, specifically diesel, now by up to 70%, what thresholds will determine the extension of similar measures today, to assist Singaporeans who rely on vehicles for their livelihoods?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The second question covers a subject that was discussed in the earlier bucket of questions, and this pertains to electricity prices for the upcoming quarters.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Given that it is really certain that these prices would be elevated and perhaps significantly elevated, does the Government intend to extend further support to households and businesses in anticipation of these higher electricity prices?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: And finally, I would like to make a point with regard to bus drivers and some small operators of transport businesses who are significantly affected by the diesel price hike and who are not included in this tranche of the Government support measures.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Because for some of them, the situation is incredibly dire.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: We very much understand the concerns of drivers and SMEs who are reliant on diesel fuel and may not have ready alternatives.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: The suggestion of whether or not to give a road tax rebate or reduction, it is too blunt a measure.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: We have, as I said in my speech earlier, aside from being a revenue measure, actually, road tax works in tandem with our other vehicle policies to achieve other longer-term outcomes, for instance, pricing in externalities related to public health and pollution, influencing vehicle buyers to choose more fuel-efficient vehicles.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: These objectives remain relevant and we do not want to go in the opposite direction.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: So, therefore, a reduction of road tax is too blunt a tool.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: We will continue to assess the situation closely, and if there is a need for us to provide further support, we can consider that at the later juncture.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: On the U-Save rebates we had initially sized them, as I mentioned, at 1.5 times the regular rate of what we normally give.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: It is to indeed cover the immediate tranche of both April to June and also subsequently from July to September, and the tranches will be disbursed in April and July respectively.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: At the moment we do not know exactly how much the fuel tariff is going to be.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: If there is a need for us to do more later, we can look at doing that as well.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: We spoke about the bus drivers earlier in relation to the earlier question by Mr Ng Chee Meng.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: Where there are bus drivers that indeed are not part of the existing package, we will work through the unions as soon as possible to provide support for this group.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: I would first like to declare my interest as head of a company that leases out taxis, limousines and private cars, before asking clarification questions.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: In particular, I am glad the Government is giving $200 to platform workers, such as food delivery personnel, taxi drivers and private hire drivers.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: But we note that this $200 is given to all platform workers regardless of their driving hours.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: There is a full-time driver who drives more than 400 kilometres a day, who apparently will get the same $200 as compared to those who drive part-time or do not drive.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Thus, I would like to ask if MOF and MOT will consider giving additional $100 or appropriate amount to drivers who drive more than eight hours a day on average, for example?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: I have a second clarification question for the Ministry of Social and Family Development (MSF).

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Many Singaporeans who receive financial assistance from a social service office will face the full brunt of the price increases and inflation.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: Of course, there are many drivers in the private hire car community that are not full-time drivers.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: They drive part time for various reasons and so, in some ways, the $200 is sized at the higher end of the range.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: We have also allowed for the fares of these services to also rise to accommodate some of these cost pressures.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: So, overall, there is a holistic cost sharing.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: We will continue to observe the situation and if there is a need for us to do more for this group, particularly the vulnerable ones, we will do so.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: I think the overall broad-based measures announced by MOF, be it the Cost-of-Living Special Payment or the U-Save rebates, although they benefit all households, but actually, they more than proportionately advantage and benefit the lower-income families.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: On this note, we think that is adequate support on that front.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: During that last review, we have built in projected inflation.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: Based on what we have observed so far, we are still within the buffer.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: And therefore, we think the ComCare assistance rates for now suffice.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: We have also pushed out the Partnership Payout, and through which we do want to encourage many of our lower-income families or ComLink+ families to come onboard the ComLink+ programme.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: With that, there is also a certain payout that can benefit our lower-income families.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: Perhaps, also allow me to respond to a question that the Member Hazlina mentioned earlier.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: I think she was alluding to the fact that many of our social service agencies have very close feelers on the ground and therefore, they understand the challenges on the ground most acutely where the needs are.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: Indeed, we agree that we want to better support our social service agencies in terms of their work, because they are best able to deliver very targeted support to the households who need those support.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: We are working closely with the social service agencies and if there is a need to reinforce their work, reinforce the support that they get, we will do so.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: It is heartening to actually know that the Government has the resources and ability to manoeuvre and assist, as compared to many countries.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: The first, many SMEs, particular, those with fixed price or longer-term contracts, lack the bargaining power to reprice quickly, even as energy, freight and material costs rise.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: I am glad to hear that Acting Minister Jeffrey Siow said the Government is taking steps to adjust pricing in major infrastructure and BTO projects.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: This is an important signal to the private sector.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Building on this approach and as a businessman, with the importance of preserving contract sanctity, if the conflict continues to indefinitely and oil prices remain elevated, whether the Government can work with and support trade associations and chambers by providing guidance, reference frameworks or industry signals that facilitate fair and timely commercial re-negotiation in exceptional circumstances.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: By increasing the Energy Efficient Grant quantum will help businesses move further as pricing on the ground has changed significantly.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Also, can we expand the Business Adaptation Grant to include advisory services that can help businesses rethink and replan their business and processes to be more energy efficient?

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: My third supplementary question is in relation to tightening credit conditions and rising working capital needs.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Will the Government consider recalibrating existing financing schemes, such as the Enterprise Financing Scheme and where relevant, the Long-Term Investment Fund and the Private Credit Growth Fund to better support SMEs facing such short-term liquidity pressures, particularly those managing volatility driven costs, or even firms that want to take this chance to basically do more mergers and acquisitions?

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: First of all, we really understand the cashflow concerns of SMEs that are caught in this current energy crisis and the price spike.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: Very much appreciative of the suggestion to involve the trade associations and chambers to support and guide businesses to get through this difficult period.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: Certainly, on behalf of the economic agencies, we will work very closely with the trade associations and chambers to do this.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: On the Energy Efficiency Grant, as I mentioned earlier, in response to another Parliamentary Question, what we do want to do is to really get out the support soon.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: So, we did not want to make significant changes to the parameters.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: But increasing the quantum of the support is something we can consider at a later juncture.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: And similarly, we will look at also the Business Adaptation Grant, which Mr Lee suggested.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: On financing support, there are not a lot of signs today that the financing ecosystem has severely tightened up.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: We need to help companies in fact, move through this transition phase quickly, continue to be energy efficient; in fact, to be more energy efficient if they can, and through some of our schemes to encourage them to do so through buying more equipment and things like that, like for example, through the Energy Efficiency Grant.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I am glad to know that we have put together a substantial first response and that the Government has drawer plans to be deployed in the mid to long term to support Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Beyond shorter-term measures, many in the broad middle are concerned about whether their wages can keep pace with the more volatile and uncertain economic and inflationary environment.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Could the Government share its plans to work with employers and unions to support sustainable wage growth and job security for mid-career and middle-income workers so that they do not slowly slip towards vulnerability over time?

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Going further, will the Government keep track of economic stress indicators among the broad middle, such as rising unsecured debt, mortgage strain or increased reliance on informal help?

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: And how will these signals inform whether more calibrated support for this group is needed if the current Middle East situation drags on for longer than expected?

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Before my next clarification, I would like to declare that I am the executive director of a social service agency that serves children from lower-income families.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Passengers, such as lower-income shift workers, caregivers and those in essential services often have the least flexibility to change their travel patterns when global events occur and fuel-linked costs rise, not just for public transport, but also for private hire transport.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In its medium- and longer-term plans for navigating this crisis and designing any transport-related interventions, how will MOT and the Government ensure long-term affordability for lower-income or vulnerable transport relief to those with no realistic ability to substitute or reduce usage?

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: What I will just say is that these are important concerns for our Government, and from a government's point of view, we will continue to work on these issues to make sure that we have a society that is well-supported and that their needs are well met.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: But more importantly, if there are people who cannot afford transport, we will find ways to support them.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: Even for large families who need to take private hire vehicles, we have additional subsidies that we have worked in through the Large Family LifeSG Credits.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: Overall, we will continue to make sure that transportation is affordable for our Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: And for the diesel vehicles, most are actually commercial vehicles.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In this this regard, if you look at the impact to sole proprietorships or micro and SMEs, the impact could be quite hard.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In the spirit of not using blunt tools, I was wondering if there are specific measures to small businesses that have diesel vehicles to mitigate the impact of higher fuel costs.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I do note the point about the enhanced Corporate Income Tax rebate.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: And if you look at the cash run component, it has been increased to about $2,000, basically an increase of $500.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: But some estimates have it that just the monthly fuel cost increase for one diesel van alone is already $172 a month.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Second, Minister Tan last month encouraged all of us to conserve energy.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Deputy Prime Minister and Prime Minister have also said the same.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: But if I look at the electricity demand in Singapore, households represent just about 6% of electricity demand based on the latest numbers.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In this regard, in terms of looking at the industrial and commercial uses, which is the overwhelming use of energy demand, what specific measures are there to have targeted measures to encourage these companies to step up on their minimum energy efficiency standards or energy conservation measures?

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: So, I will just add a little bit more to the answer.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: I think that even if we do cut diesel tax duties, it might not necessarily pass through fully to the end consumer.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: Therefore, it is not really the best way to try to convey help directly to the people who need it the most.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: More importantly, as I said earlier, we do not want to blunt the price signals and reduce the incentive for the longer-term objective, which is to encourage actually businesses to switch to more energy efficient modes of transport, as well as to be more efficient in how they use their vehicles.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: How would the Ministry of Health (MOH) be mitigating this, so that some of these costs are not passed on to consumers, therefore inflating and exacerbating healthcare prices and costs?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: The second question is whether in in light of the current situation, is there any impact on whether it is our stockpile or supply of critical medicines, or maybe certain specialty areas?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: On the impact of the disruption, there is an immediate impact, which is supply we procure that comes through the Strait of Hormuz.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: One ingredient is helium, and I explained earlier, the impact is not big because we do not take our helium from there.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But I think what we need to watch out for is the secondary domino effect.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Because if petrochemical products are disrupted, then the raw materials to make gloves, syringes will be affected.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Korea is affected because they make their own syringes.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We import from suppliers, so, for now, we are not affected.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: If chemicals used to make drug substances are impacted, then drug suppliers will be impacted.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The global supply chain is actually not a chain, it is a very intricate web.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We need to monitor those downstream domino effects.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I think Acting Minister Jeffrey Siow has mentioned that temporary assistance will be provided for those who need them for essential services.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: For many of these vulnerable groups, for example, the elderly, the disabled, the younger disabled, those who are in special education schools and so forth, they have very few alternatives in terms of transport mode.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I worry that if the measures are too blunt or too low even after co-funding, the service providers who chose to provide essential transport services for this group might choose to exit.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: That is something that we do not want to see because it does create more hardship.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: So, I want to ask if the relevant Ministries, for example, the Ministry of Education (MOE), MSF and MOH, who are supporting this group, before they make their final decision and announce them, can you do a more detailed study in terms of the impact and perhaps look at tiering some of these measures before announcing them, and provide a space to have flexibility for those who are truly undergoing hardship or will create hardship, to protect the vulnerable who have few alternatives and also to preserve those service providers who have other alternatives to make money but choose to serve this group of vulnerable people?

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: Indeed, we want to absolutely ensure that these critical services continue to be operated for the vulnerable.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: And on behalf of those agencies that she mentioned, we will make sure that we take care of the vulnerable and the services continue to be run.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: And we will consult all relevant stakeholders to make sure that this is so.

speaker: Mr Goh Pei Ming
text: I just wanted to add that at this current juncture, as we speak, MOF, together with MOE, MSF as well as MOH, are working on the details following up from what has been disseminated today.

speaker: Mr Goh Pei Ming
text: I think the timeliness of it should allow us to provide increased subsidy rates as well as expanded coverage for families.

speaker: Mr Goh Pei Ming
text: This, hopefully, will come at a good time whereby it provides additional support for some of these families that we are speaking about.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The Singapore Department of Statistics publishes retail prices and what consumers pay at the end.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: I am not sure we track the full cost structure behind the prices – domestic supply chain margins, domestic transport, wholesale margins, retail margins and so on.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: If you do not have a baseline understanding of the cost structure before the prices rise further, you will not be able to tell later whether a price increase was done by genuine cost pressures or by margin expansion.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Will the Government establish baseline cost structure data now for key categories such as food, transport and energy companies, especially the retail-facing ones?

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: I just want to explain that we operate our economy in a very competitive manner.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We just want to make sure that in our retail market and wholesale market, we have sufficient competition to allow businesses to operate in a competitive way.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: This way is the best way to ensure that our prices are reasonable.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: For those who are taking advantage of the market to try to raise the prices, there will be competitors, they will compete to offer alternatives.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: This is the best way to ensure that our prices are always reasonable and competitive.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: If there is a lack of competition, then the Commission will intervene where necessary.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am sure many Singaporean vulnerable households and businesses are grateful for the short-term measures that we have announced and brought forward.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But as we know, it will never be enough and there will always be opportunities to do more.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: At a recent residents' dialogue, I came across some opinions that the crisis is not that severe, having seen other countries where they have had fuel shortages and even electricity supply cuts.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is something that we need to be mindful of.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am very heartened that among the residents, the younger generation made some very interesting suggestions – that perhaps the Government can go beyond a crisis and a money solution, to go beyond money to rally our people.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is a crisis that falls not just on Singapore, but across the whole world.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Perhaps the Government can consider some measures to bring out people together nationally so that they feel they can also do their part to contribute.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For example, to conserve electricity in a more objective way.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: So, can the Government consider a campaign to bring our Singaporeans together to contribute to this solution, over and above just money being given out?

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: I want to thank Mr Victor Lye for his suggestion.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Indeed, communication and engagement are an important part of the work of the committee.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We do want to reach out to take this opportunity to re-emphasise the importance of conservation and to share with Singaporeans the situation regularly so that they are updated on the situation that we are facing.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: This is indeed a crisis and it is a crisis serious enough for us to set up the HCMC to oversee this whole-of-Government effort to manage the crisis.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Today, we have three Ministerial Statements, which also signifies the importance of this crisis situation.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: This is something that we hope to be able to reach out to our people.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: The Member's suggestions about campaigns and exercises are something that we will consider.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Where practical and where it is meaningful, we will be happy to work with the community or community organisations, we will work with schools, we will work with trade associations to see how we can continue to re-emphasise this message of a crisis situation and that we need to do our part to continue to conserve all our resources – energy, food, water and all the important resources.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Ten years on, we now face a global oil price surge.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Will the Government consider a temporary freeze of foreign worker levies to affected sectors, especially the construction sector?

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: This will directly help to offset the impact of rising costs.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: And if the crisis prolongs, were there be alternative support measures to help these businesses manage this cost as well?

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: This include businesses who manage private contracts who will not be able to benefit from BCA's co-sharing of fuel calls for key Government projects.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: At this particular point in time, we are monitoring the situation very closely.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Our first priority would be to support all of our fresh graduates who are graduating.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We are also concerned about the potential of AI disruptions on fresh graduates looking and landing jobs.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Just by cutting away the levy completely, without any concomitant tie-backs to increase productivity and value-add, I think we are going to set ourselves back.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: A couple of clarifications and suggestions, if I may.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: Looking at the critical nature of this situation, will the Government be imposing a curb on private transportation use as what other countries have been deploying, in Malaysia and Indonesia?

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: The whole idea is to reduce our consumption and plan further when the urgency is needed.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: Number two is that if you look at the Energy Efficiency Grant and if we are relying on households to reduce their consumption, if I may recommend that we reward reduced consumption?

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: Because only then will the value of using energy more efficiently be taken into account.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: If typically, their consumption is $100 a month and they manage to reduce it by $20, a percentage of that can be returned to them as a reward.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: I think that puts Singaporeans in a mindset of using energy wisely, in terms of how we can encourage the efficiency of consumption.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: Thirdly, looking at this situation of energy dependency, it is important to ensure we are energy independent.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: On the acceleration, the last point from the Member about the deployment of small modular reactors, I believe I have answered it quite extensively.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Perhaps just to reiterate: we are doing everything we can.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We have shared with everyone here about the four switches in terms of the diversification of our energy sources to achieve some measure of energy independence.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We have gone on this Decarbonisation Grand Challenge, which was announced at the Committee of Supply this year to look for low-carbon technologies.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: And to try to see how we can use biomethane as a sandbox.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, we are trying everything there is, including exploring geothermal.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: And the last bit is a question of waiting for the first of a kind to be operational and to be deployed and to be safe before we start to adopt.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We have sent our teams to learn from the US.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Our teams have gone to the US multiple times to look at the different centres in Idaho, in Oak Ridge and in Boston as well.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: At the same time, we have tie-ups with the United Arab Emirates.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Of course, at this particular point in time, no one is there from our side.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We have also signed agreements with the Koreans, with the Japanese, with the United Kingdom and the French to learn from them on some of these advanced nuclear technologies.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: And we are also working very closely with the International Atomic Energy Agency to see how we can self-evaluate through the Integrated Nuclear Infrastructure Review.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: And we will keep this House posted very regularly on the accelerated pathways that we have adopted to reach that energy independence.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Those are the measures that I have articulated many, many times.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: To the Member's point about whether we should consider rationing power use, for instance.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We do not want to cause panic because we are actually stable.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We also do not want to cause panic to investors, to the world economy, to our downstream partner countries whom we export refined products to.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: But at some point in time, as part and parcel of Total Defence Day, we may do an exercise to test out the readiness when it comes to power rationing.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: If I may borrow your time, since we are here.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: You are all respectively advisors of your constituencies, your Group Representation Constituencies (GRCs) and so on.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: If you can adopt energy saving measures across the entire GRC, we would really welcome that.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: And I want to make a shout-out to the Senior Parliamentary Secretary Shawn Huang.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I think in his constituency he adopted energy-saving motion sensor lighting in the HDB blocks.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: To also address the Member Louis Chua's point about the fact that domestic use is a very small amount, but it hits the pocket.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, we are trying on multiple prongs to get our population, our businesses, our country, our society as a whole to adopt energy conservation as its core, as its foundation.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: And in fact, that is the very reason why we do not want to reduce diesel or fuel taxes and duties.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: But our context is quite different from other countries.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: We, as Dr Tan explained, are not facing a shortage of fuel.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: What we are facing are high fuel prices and that in itself, should be an incentive for people to drive less, and maybe, hopefully to use public transport more.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: I would just want to just add very quickly that the situation that we have is a position of strength.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: We are here, fortunate that we are discussing how to cope with higher fuel prices, rather than discussing whether we are running out of fuel.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: We allow the price mechanism to function, so that energy is priced properly in Singapore and used efficiently.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: They allow us to be in a strong position to act, not just react, so that we are able to cope with these crises.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: And it is all because we have a good Government that is prepared, anticipates problems and plans ahead for the future.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Acting Minister Siow, I recall earlier, there was a question by Mr Saktiandi Supaat.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: You might want to respond to his earlier question.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: One is whether or not the inflationary impact can be mitigated with our use of our monetary policies.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: And to that end, indeed, MAS will look at this as part of its regular review of monetary policies.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: I think we will see what they will intend to do in the coming months.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: I think his other question was about off-Budget measures and whether or not we have plans to do that.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: As I have explained in my speech, we do have drawer plans.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: If the situation changes and if needed, we will indeed activate them and bring them together as off-Budget measures if needed.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: I am not at liberty to give too much details on what it is, because this is as part of national security; I think we want to keep that on our own books.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Having said that, I think we are in a better position today, having had learnt from COVID-19, from the last energy crisis, to be able to diversify our sources.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: So, hence, today, while we are not impacted, while we are not likely to see food disruptions in the short term, we cannot fully insulate ourselves from increases in food prices; as a result of increases, such as fertilisers and other food inputs.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: So, I think this is where a lot of the measures as covered by MOF earlier, provide assurance in the short term that the Government is looking into this.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: And if I can assure Members too, that perhaps, like Mr Victor Lye had suggested earlier, make this a learning moment.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: If I can also pitch for our local farmers and local production, this is also a time for us to build our local capabilities, our local farming resilience.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: For us to also look into buying local produce, that helps our farms to increase capacity at this point, helps them build resilience over time and should there be disruptions or should there be a need for us to divert supplies or look to ramp up local production, I think they would be in a better position if we do what we can today to support them too.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: So, this is, I think, one learning moment that we can do.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: And I hope that the community can come forth and support our local farmers this round.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Will there be any plans to provide targeted support like rental or utility rebates for our hawkers and our stallholders as they strive to continue providing affordable meals for Singaporeans?

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: I think on the hawker front, we keep our rentals as low as possible to sustain our hawkers.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: But for food prices, we continue to monitor.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: My colleague, Minister of State Gan mentioned about how we are monitoring food supply of food prices, and I think that we will continue to do so.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: The current measures are what we look at, in terms of CDC vouchers and special payments.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: I think that is where we look to support households in the meantime and we will keep everyone posted should there be changes.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: But rest assured we are monitoring, we are engaging our hawkers.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: We will try to keep prices as competitive and low as possible, but I cannot guarantee that there will not be food price increases as a result of, what I shared earlier.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: We are importing most of our food supply and so, we are not insulated against food hikes or food prices as a result of the global situation right now.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: I was wondering whether there could be some support, like rental or utility rebates for them.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: There is no need at this juncture, because we have not seen the price hikes hit the hawkers in the same way as yet.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: I think we have already had enough explanations and elaborations from MTI colleagues on energy price hikes at this point.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: I think we are still in stable mode.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: So, if the need arises, rest assured that the Ministry will provide the necessary assistance as required.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: I have two cluster of questions and one suggestion.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: With rising input costs, how might this translate into food prices in our school canteens?

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Will MOE work with stallholders to monitor and manage price increase?

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: And should there be any price adjustment, would this be communicated to parents, because what I hear from parents, this is so that they are able to make informed decisions to adjust pocket money for their children.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: The second cluster of question relates to MOT.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: In my interaction with private hires with Minister of State Rahayu Mahzam recently, many of them raised concerns about their fuel costs.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: And with this $200 support, it will help to cushion these pressures.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: One thing I have learnt in my role and caring for Clementi residents, is that, in times of need and time of fear and crises, scammers will leverage on this to tell our residents to do things that will put them in a vulnerable position.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: So, my suggestion is, could we also in this period of time, increase our advisory on scams and also for all of us, as we interact with our residents to let them know to be mindful for any advisories that come to them that they should always double check and also dial 1799 for any clarification.

speaker: Mr Jeffrey Siow
text: I think that is the best way to do it, rather than try to blunt the price signals by giving them a long-term fuel subsidy.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: That was addressed by Senior Minister of State Zaqy.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: But I also thought that in relation to what she asked, another area where people might be concerned about could be the HDB coffee shops, because that is also where they buy their meals.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: So, if like what Senior Minister of State Zaqy said, we would monitor the situation, and if there is a need for us to sync up what we do with regard to rental costs to help with how hawkers or coffeeshop operators are doing, then we will do so.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I am going to move to the third bucket, on security and related matters.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I wanted to follow up on the thrust of my Parliamentary Question Nos 15 and 62.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: First clarification, could the Minister please clarify whether the Government is planning on the basis that the current disruptions are temporary, or are we entering into a period of structurally more permanent and more volatile global environment?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: For example, between resilience and cost competitiveness, someone has to pay for resilience, or between targeted support and more broad-based coverage.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Could the Minister provide specific indications on the thresholds that the Government is monitoring, not in the context of price caps, as Minister of State Gan addressed earlier, but in energy prices, duration of disruptions, cost increases in certain sectors?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: So, what would trigger a shift in the policy response?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: And lastly, beyond the tactical immediate stabilisation measures, what are the longer-term structural changes that the Government is considering, taking into account that we do have the restructuring committee's recommendations that are also coming out, but what are the current assessments on the biggest gaps or limitations that the Government may have, in terms of policies, as we shift to a more permanently volatile environment?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: And I ask this in the context of both being resilient in a defensive way, but also in an offensive way.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: So, the current policies are great at making it easy to do business, but do we need to shift more to, for example, thinking about how we assess risks, or how we share risks, as well as rewards, in a more volatile environment?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Although it is back to the first bucket.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: I think this is regarding security and long-term strategy.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: First and foremost, I think this crisis is temporary – in a sense, and all crises are temporary, But I think the impact of this crisis will be quite long lasting.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: First, it reminds us that the geopolitical situation landscape has changed and it is important for us to understand the implications of that.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: And that also relates to your second question, with regard to a trade-off between resilience and cost.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: I think many years ago, our focus has been efficiency.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Our focus has been in cost effectiveness, just-in-time delivery and production.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: But I think over the last few years, with the multiple crises that we have been confronted with, including COVID-19 and now, this oil crisis, energy crisis, it reminds us that it is not just about "just in time", it is also "just in case".

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: So, therefore, it is important for us to review our policy, our strategy, our approach, to ensure carefully calibrated balance between resilience and at the same time, competitiveness.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: There will always be trade-offs in terms of cost, if you want to have a greater security.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: I think even in today's world, when we talk about energy security, we talk about stockpile for our energy requirement, stockpile will cost money.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: And even if we enter into long-term contracts, long-term contracts will also have a premium versus a spot market in situations when there is a volatility.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: At the same time, when we look at the cost increase, as a result of disruptions in supply chain, it is something that we also have to always bear in mind.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: And if we talk about the security for our oil dependent sectors, particularly our refineries, we talk about the access to crude and the need for us to explore alternative sources, and we talk about supplies from outside the Middle East, which will be more costly and take longer to deliver – all these are balances that we need to recalibrate, in response to the changing environment in the geopolitical outlook.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: If we are able to move fast, decisively, into embracing AI and adopting AI, and becoming an AI leader, I think that will give us an added competitive edge versus our competition.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: At the same time, I also talked about, in my speech earlier, that we need to continue to strengthen our partnership with our like-minded partners – other countries, other economies – to see how we can cooperate and create more space for us, and by international cooperation, that would also strengthen our economic resilience.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: So, I think it is a multi-pronged approach, it is not a single strategy.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: But all these, what we are putting in place, I also need to remind all of us that these strategies must continue to evolve and change, because the global environment is changing all the time.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: The Economic Strategy Review Committee report will not be the final review of our economy; I think it is an ongoing process.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Hopefully, we run slightly faster than our competitors.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: And will it be stepping up our cyber defence stance above the baseline level during this period?

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I believe you would have read in the news that both our Prime Ministers, Prime Minister Wong and Prime Minister Anwar, they have been in phone calls as well.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: And every opportunity that we have, we discuss how to collaborate more – between the whole ASEAN member state framework and also, the fact that we are the closest neighbours.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: For Australia, just like the ASEAN member states, because of the interdependence, given our position as a global hub and particularly, a Southeast Asia hub for refineries, our downstream products are equally in demand, just like their natural gas is also equally in demand by us.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, I think that mutual dependency serves both on a multilateral basis well; and we continue to build on those.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Those are the measures that we have today and I believe that they have served us well all these decades.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Like what Deputy Prime Minister has just shared, the world is also changing rapidly.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Right now, everyone is looking at "just in case".

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I believe that as a result of this particular crisis, some degree of scarring is bound to happen and there will be countries who will start to hoard as well.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: But I think for us, we continue to remain clear-headed, consistent in the way we deal with all of our neighbours and with all of our partners.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We continue to be transparent and maintain our credibility.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I believe that it is not just working within the ASEAN framework, it is also working with Northeast Asia partners – Japan, Republic of Korea, China; working with Oceania, which is Australia, New Zealand; working with the Middle East.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Because at some point in time, this crisis will also abate, and of course, opening up new markets.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: That has always been what we have been carrying out all this while.

speaker: The Minister for Digital Development and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: When a conflict of this nature takes place, naturally, we have to watch out for potential vectors of attack, even if Singapore is not directly involved in the theatre of action.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Minister Balakrishnan, would you like to respond to Mr Fadli Fauzi's earlier question?

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Singapore's position on straits used for international navigation is long-standing and consistent.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: The Strait of Hormuz, just like the Straits of Malacca and Singapore, are examples of straits used for international navigation.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: No "ifs", no "buts", no questions – as far as we are concerned, it is so.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: What is the international law position on these types of straits?

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: It is not a privilege to be granted by the bordering state.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: It is not a licence to be supplicated for.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: It is not a toll to be paid.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Singapore also takes the position that this right of transit passage, is also part of customary international law.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: And in case you are wondering why I am nitpicking about "customary international law", it is because there are some other states that may have signed but have not ratified UNCLOS, and I am stating that, so that I am telling you this is not a "get out of jail free" card for states that have not ratified UNCLOS.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: So, we have been closely monitoring the situation in the Strait of Hormuz.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: The Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore remains in close contact with the ship owners, as well as the operators of Singapore-flagged or Singapore-registered ships in the Persian Gulf.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: At both the international and regional levels, our agencies are engaging with the stakeholders to explore potential opportunities to facilitate safe transit of the ships.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: And do not forget, there is also a humanitarian issue for the workers, for the maritime sailors onboard these ships.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: This includes engaging the International Maritime Organization (IMO) and the member states on the potential establishment of a safe maritime corridor following the 36th Extraordinary Session of the IMO Council.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: In addition, we are also engaging regional counterparts on other possible arrangements that may be explored.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: You may be wondering why I am taking such a legal and strict definition.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: It is not because I am particularly obsessed with law but because the Straits of Malacca and Singapore is, in fact, another critical chokepoint.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: The Member may be aware that, in fact, if you add up all the maritime oil, crude and refined, you might be surprised that actually, more flows through the Straits of Malacca and Singapore than even the Strait of Hormuz.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: If we think about global trade, container trade – there has far more flowing through this place.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
